profiles.name: Benjamin E. Mays
profiles.blurb: Benjamin Elijah Mays was a Baptist minister, educator, scholar, and outspoken critic of segregation. As Morehouse College president from 1940 to 1967, he mentored Martin Luther King Jr. and helped shape the language and moral framework of the civil-rights movement. He later chaired Atlanta’s school board during school desegregation. Mays was first buried at South-View; his remains were moved to Morehouse in 1995.
profiles.credit: Portrait by Robert Templeton; courtesy of Tim Templeton via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).
profiles.license: CC BY-SA 4.0

profiles.name: William H. Crogman
profiles.blurb: Born in Philipsburg on Sint Maarten, William Henry Crogman became a classicist and educator in the United States. After teaching at Claflin, he joined Clark University in Atlanta in 1876, became a senior professor, and served as Clark’s president from 1903 to 1910. He advocated education and equal citizenship and taught at Clark for decades.
profiles.credit: William H. Crogman portrait, Atlanta University Photographs, Robert W. Woodruff Library, via Digital Library of Georgia.
profiles.license: Public domain in the United States (published before 1931)

profiles.name: Robert Grant
profiles.blurb: Robert Grant was a blacksmith, drayman, minister, and community organizer in post-Civil-War Atlanta. He helped organize Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872 and was among the Black businessmen who established South-View Cemetery, creating a dignified burial ground under segregation. Zion Hill’s history says Grant died in 1896; an exact date of birth or death was not found.
profiles.license: No reuse license found; obtain permission from Zion Hill Baptist Church Archives before publishing.

profiles.name: Grace Towns Hamilton
profiles.blurb: Grace Towns Hamilton was an Atlanta educator, Urban League leader, and politician who became the first Black woman elected to Georgia’s General Assembly. She led the Atlanta Urban League, worked on housing, education, health, and voter-registration issues, and later served in the legislature from 1966 to 1985. Her career made her a key bridge between Atlanta’s civic reform networks and state politics.
profiles.license: Archive item has no clear reuse license in the record; obtain permission before publishing.

profiles.name: Alonzo Herndon
profiles.blurb: Born enslaved in Walton County, Alonzo Franklin Herndon built a successful barbering business in Atlanta and became one of the city’s leading Black entrepreneurs. In 1905 he acquired the Atlanta Benevolent and Protective Association, the foundation of Atlanta Life Insurance Company, which became one of the country’s major Black-owned insurers. His business, philanthropy, and civic support strengthened Atlanta’s Black community.
profiles.credit: Alonzo Herndon portrait, source image from Sweet Auburn; via Wikimedia Commons.
profiles.license: Public domain in the United States (Commons PD-US determination)

profiles.name: Annie L. McPheeters
profiles.blurb: Annie Lou McPheeters was a librarian, educator, and advocate for African American history and culture. At Atlanta’s Auburn Branch Library she developed adult education programming and established the Negro History Collection, later moving with the collection to West Hunter Branch. She supported library desegregation and helped make research materials available to Black communities who had long been excluded from public resources.
profiles.license: No explicit image reuse license found on the archive record; request permission from Auburn Avenue Research Library.

profiles.name: John W. Dobbs
profiles.blurb: John Wesley Dobbs was an Atlanta civic and political leader known as the unofficial “Mayor of Auburn Avenue.” A railway mail clerk for more than three decades, he helped build Black political power through voter registration and organizations including the Atlanta Negro Voters League. His organizing helped press for the hiring of Atlanta’s first Black police officers in 1948 and influenced the city’s civil-rights movement.

profiles.name: Graham W. Jackson Sr.
profiles.blurb: Graham Washington Jackson Sr. was an Atlanta musician and bandleader known for virtuoso performances on organ, piano, and accordion. After moving to Atlanta to attend Morehouse in 1924, he formed the Seminole Syncopators and built a long career performing for presidents and audiences across the country. A familiar figure in Atlanta music, he also served on Georgia’s State Board of Corrections and was named the state’s official musician by Governor Jimmy Carter.
profiles.license: No explicit reuse license found; request permission from Auburn Avenue Research Library.

profiles.name: Ludie Clay Andrews
profiles.blurb: Ludie Clay Andrews was a pioneering Atlanta nurse and nursing educator. After graduating from Spelman’s MacVicar Hospital nurse-training program in 1906, she led hospital training programs and worked to open Georgia’s nursing profession to Black women. Following a decade-long campaign, Black nurses gained access to state registration in 1919–1920, and Andrews became Georgia’s first Black registered nurse. She is buried at South-View.
profiles.license: No explicit image reuse license found; permission required.

profiles.name: Bazoline E. Usher
profiles.blurb: Bazoline Estelle Usher spent more than four decades teaching Black students in Atlanta’s segregated public schools. She became the first Black director and supervisor of Negro schools in Atlanta and the first African American with an office at City Hall. In 1943 she organized Girl Scout troops for Black girls, expanding leadership and recreation opportunities when many institutions excluded them.
profiles.credit: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-DIG-cph-3d02231.
profiles.license: Public domain in the United States (U.S. publication before 1931)

profiles.name: John Lewis
profiles.blurb: John Lewis was a civil-rights organizer whose activism began in the Nashville sit-ins and Freedom Rides and brought him to the leadership of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. On Bloody Sunday in 1965, Alabama state troopers beat Lewis and other marchers as they crossed Selma’s Edmund Pettus Bridge. He later represented Georgia’s Fifth District in Congress for more than three decades and became known as the “conscience of Congress.” He was buried at South-View before reinterment at the King Center.
profiles.credit: U.S. Congress, official portrait of Congressman John Lewis (public domain).
profiles.license: Public domain (U.S. federal government work)

profiles.name: Dr. Moses Amos
profiles.blurb: Moses Amos became Georgia’s first licensed Black pharmacist and a prominent Atlanta druggist. He opened Gate City Drug Store, a Black-owned pharmacy serving the city’s African American community, and spent decades filling prescriptions and building an independent business. The South-View Preservation Foundation describes his career as spanning roughly fifty years; an exact birth or death day was not established in this research.
profiles.license: Historical periodical image; Commons file page/license needs confirmation before reuse.

profiles.name: Dinah Watts Pace
profiles.blurb: Born enslaved in Georgia, Dinah Watts Pace pursued education at Atlanta University and became a teacher and community institution-builder. In Covington she founded a school and a home for children without parents, educating hundreds of young people over the course of decades. Her work connected schooling, care, and community leadership during Reconstruction and its aftermath.
profiles.credit: Mrs. Dinah Watts Pace, in Lawson Andrew Scruggs, Women of Distinction (1893), via Wikimedia Commons.
profiles.license: Public domain in the United States (published 1893)

profiles.name: Freddye Henderson
profiles.blurb: Freddye Scarborough Henderson was an Atlanta entrepreneur, educator, columnist, and travel pioneer. She and her husband opened Henderson Travel Service in 1955, building a Black-owned agency that organized international travel at a time when Black travelers faced discrimination. In 1957 she arranged a group trip to Ghana for that country’s independence celebrations, helping open international travel routes and experiences for African American clients.
profiles.license: No explicit reuse license found; obtain permission from AARL before publishing.

profiles.name: Carolyn D. Yancey
profiles.blurb: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey was an educator and civic leader who taught in Detroit before settling in Atlanta. She was elected to the Atlanta Board of Education in 1982 and served for sixteen years, contributing to education policy and community institutions. Her papers and photographs document a life of public service alongside her husband, Atlanta civic leader Asa G. Yancey.
profiles.license: No explicit reuse license found for the photographs; obtain permission before publishing.

profiles.name: Geneva Haugabrooks
profiles.blurb: Geneva Haugabrooks was an Atlanta entrepreneur and educator who became known for her funeral and business enterprises and for public service in the city’s Black community. South-View’s profile lists her as an entrepreneur and teacher; this search did not establish authoritative exact life dates or a sufficiently documented milestone to add a dated event. Obtain a cemetery or archival biography before writing a fuller page.
profiles.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (noncommercial use only; no derivatives); check project use and get permission if uncertain.

profiles.name: Horace Mann Bond
profiles.blurb: Horace Mann Bond was a historian, education researcher, and college administrator whose work challenged racist claims about Black intelligence and documented the history of Black education. He led Fort Valley State College and Lincoln University before returning to Atlanta University as dean and research director. His research for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund contributed to the evidentiary context for Brown v. Board of Education; he was also the father of civil-rights leader Julian Bond.
profiles.license: Commons lists public domain due non-renewal, but file has been nominated for deletion over licensing; resolve/verify before use.

profiles.name: Jean Childs Young
profiles.blurb: Jean Childs Young was an educator and advocate for children’s rights who also participated in the civil-rights movement. She developed citizenship-school curriculum for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and joined voter-registration work and major demonstrations, including the 1963 March on Washington and the Selma-to-Montgomery march. As first lady of Atlanta during Andrew Young’s mayoralty, she continued her work on education and children’s issues nationally and locally.
profiles.license: No free reuse license verified for the newspaper photograph; obtain rights clearance before publication.

profiles.name: John W. E. Bowen
profiles.blurb: John Wesley Edward Bowen was a theologian, minister, scholar, and educator who became one of the first Black professors at Gammon Theological Seminary in Atlanta. He taught historical theology, later led Gammon as president, and wrote and spoke on African American history, religion, and citizenship. In 1895 he delivered “An Appeal to the King” during Negro Day at the Cotton States and International Exposition, a major public address on racial equality.
profiles.license: Public domain in the United States (1896 publication)

profiles.name: Lillian Miles Lewis
profiles.blurb: Lillian Miles Lewis was an educator and academic who worked at Atlanta University and Clark Atlanta University, and a trusted adviser to her husband, Congressman John Lewis. Her archive includes correspondence, photographs, and records connected with both her own work and her husband’s public life. She died in Atlanta in 2012; a precise date of birth was not established in this research.
profiles.license: No explicit image reuse license found; request permission from the foundation.

profiles.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
profiles.blurb: Martin Luther King Jr. was an Atlanta-born Baptist minister and central leader of the modern civil-rights movement. His leadership in the Montgomery bus boycott, nonviolent direct-action campaigns, and voting-rights organizing helped drive major changes in American law and public life. King was assassinated in Memphis in 1968 and was initially buried at South-View before his remains were moved to the King Center.
profiles.credit: New York World-Telegram and Sun Collection, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (public domain).
profiles.license: Public domain in the United States; LoC identifies no known copyright restrictions for this work-for-hire image.

events.title: Ludie Clay Andrews dies after a life in nursing
events.description: Ludie Clay Andrews died on January 6, 1969, from injuries caused by a house fire. A graduate of Spelman’s nursing program, she helped organize Grady Hospital’s Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses in 1914 and later supervised nursing at MacVicar Hospital.
events.sourceLabel: Georgia Women of Achievement: Ludie Clay Andrews

events.title: Dinah Watts Pace dies after building a home and school for children
events.description: Dinah Watts Pace died on January 25, 1933, after burns from a fire at her Covington home. Born enslaved near Athens, she completed Atlanta University’s normal course in 1883 and went to Covington to teach. There she encountered children with little access to schooling and care beyond what families could provide.
events.sourceLabel: The Covington News: Dinah Watts Pace, a Covington legend

events.title: Bazoline E. Usher dies after decades in Atlanta education
events.description: Bazoline Estelle Usher died in Atlanta on February 8, 1992, aged 106. Born in Walton County on December 26, 1885, she graduated from Atlanta University in 1906, taught in Virginia, and returned to Atlanta in 1915. She served for fourteen years as principal of David T. Howard High School before supervising the city’s Black schools under segregation.
events.sourceLabel: Georgia Women of Achievement: Bazoline E. Usher

events.title: Bloody Sunday: John Lewis and marchers are attacked in Selma
events.description: On March 7, 1965, John Lewis and Hosea Williams led hundreds of peaceful voting-rights marchers out of Selma toward Montgomery. At the Edmund Pettus Bridge, Alabama state troopers and deputized men ordered them to turn back, then attacked with clubs and tear gas. Lewis suffered a fractured skull. Images of the violence carried the marchers’ demand for voting rights to a national audience; President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act that August.
events.sourceLabel: National Archives: Selma Marches

events.title: Harriet Graham dies and is buried at South-View
events.description: Harriet Graham, widow of South-View founder George Graham and a shareholder in the cemetery herself, was found dead at her Fraser Street home on March 31, 1904. A coroner’s jury initially attributed her death to heart disease. Investigators then learned that an anonymous miniature coffin containing a threatening message had been left at her door.
events.source: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 15, OCR page estimate 174 (printed page near 159).
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 159–160; catalog record

events.title: Graham Jackson plays as Roosevelt’s body leaves Warm Springs
events.description: On April 13, 1945, Graham Jackson played “Goin’ Home” on accordion as Franklin D. Roosevelt’s body was carried from the Little White House toward the train at Warm Springs. Jackson had performed for Roosevelt many times. Life photographer Ed Clark captured him weeping beside the procession, creating one of the best-known photographs of the president’s death.
events.sourceLabel: University of Georgia Libraries: Graham Jackson and the Warm Springs procession

events.title: South-View Cemetery receives its charter
events.description: Georgia approved the South-View Cemetery Association’s charter on April 21, 1886. Six Black Atlanta businessmen and civic leaders—Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Robert Grant, Charles H. Morgan, Albert Watts, and John Render—had applied to create a burial ground that Black Atlantans could own and govern. Grant, a blacksmith and drayman, had also helped establish Zion Hill Baptist Church and served as its founding pastor.
events.sourceLabel: Zion Hill Baptist Church: Rev. Robert Grant and South-View’s charter

events.title: Henry Rutherford Butler calls for care of South-View’s grounds
events.description: On May 6, 1900, physician and civic leader Henry Rutherford Butler used his Atlanta Constitution column to urge South-View lot owners to keep their family plots maintained. The appeal asked readers to make the grounds “green and clean,” turning grave care into a shared responsibility for the cemetery’s future.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), chapter 6; catalog record

events.title: The 1902 Pittsburgh siege and mob violence
events.description: On May 17, 1902, a confrontation between Will Richardson, a Black Pittsburgh resident, and Samuel Kerlin, a white former Atlanta police officer, escalated into an armed siege. Richardson retreated to his store and residence on Amy Street, where he exchanged gunfire with police as a crowd gathered. The fighting continued into the next day; three policemen, another white man, and two Black men, including Richardson, were killed. A white mob threatened to burn the neighborhood, and fire destroyed a block of Amy Street.
events.source: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 11, section “The Pittsburgh Riot,” OCR page estimate 130–134 (printed pages around 116–119).
events.sourceLabel: National Register of Historic Places: Pittsburgh Historic District nomination

events.title: Henry Ossian Flipper is buried at South-View
events.description: Henry Ossian Flipper was buried at South-View on May 17, 1940, after dying in Atlanta at his brother Joseph’s home. Born enslaved in Thomasville, he became the first African American to graduate from West Point, in 1877, and served as an officer with the 10th Cavalry. At Fort Sill he designed a drainage system that reduced the stagnant water blamed for malaria.
events.source: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 11, OCR page estimate 128.
events.sourceLabel: National Park Service: Henry O. Flipper

events.title: Atlanta buries AME bishop Henry McNeal Turner
events.description: Henry McNeal Turner’s body arrived in Atlanta after he died in Windsor, Ontario, while traveling on church business. On May 19, 1915, Big Bethel AME Church filled for his funeral, and a procession carried him to South-View. Turner had spent decades building AME congregations in Georgia; he had also served as a Union Army chaplain and, during Reconstruction, as one of Georgia’s Black legislators.
events.sourceLabel: New Georgia Encyclopedia: Henry McNeal Turner

events.title: Grace Towns Hamilton dies after a career in Georgia politics
events.description: Grace Towns Hamilton died on June 17, 1992, after a career that moved from civil-rights administration into state politics. As executive director of the Atlanta Urban League from 1943 to 1961, she worked on housing, education, health services, and voter registration for Black residents. Her approach sought concrete gains within segregation, a strategy that eventually brought her into conflict with the national Urban League.
events.sourceLabel: New Georgia Encyclopedia: Grace Towns Hamilton

events.title: Atlanta honors poet, painter, and minister Thomas Jefferson Flanagan
events.description: Atlanta City Council proclaimed July 6, 1983, Dr. Thomas Jefferson Flanagan Day. By then Flanagan had spent decades writing for the city’s Black press: he worked with the Atlanta Independent and joined the Atlanta Daily World’s editorial staff soon after the paper began publication in 1928. His work included editorials, poetry, and books such as The Road to Mount McKeithan and The Canyons at Providence.
events.sourceLabel: Atlanta Daily World obituary, Georgia State University Digital Collections

events.title: Alonzo Herndon dies, leaving Atlanta Life to the next generation
events.description: Alonzo Herndon died in Atlanta on July 21, 1927, after building a business spanning barbering, real estate, and insurance. Born enslaved in Walton County on June 26, 1858, he learned the barber’s trade and reached Atlanta in 1883. His barbershops served elite white customers, and he invested the proceeds in property and new businesses.
events.sourceLabel: New Georgia Encyclopedia: Alonzo Herndon

events.title: Mount Olivet pastor William R. Clemmons dies from gunshot injuries
events.description: William R. Clemmons, pastor of Atlanta’s Mount Olivet Baptist Church, died on July 26, 1887, six days after being shot in the leg on his way home from prayer meeting. Three men confronted him; after he escaped into a church member’s home, the wound worsened and an amputation failed to save him. The attackers and motive were never established.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead

events.title: Benjamin E. Mays begins his Morehouse presidency
events.description: Morehouse College appointed Benjamin E. Mays president on August 1, 1940. The son of parents who had been enslaved in South Carolina, Mays had studied at Bates College and the University of Chicago, become a Baptist minister, and led Howard University’s School of Religion. He would remain at Morehouse for twenty-seven years, shaping the college during a period when Black institutions carried much of the burden of higher education under segregation.
events.sourceLabel: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute: Mays appointed Morehouse president

events.title: South-View trustees ask Atlanta to waive a cemetery license fee
events.description: During the financial panic of 1893, South-View’s trustees asked Atlanta’s city council to waive the cemetery’s $100 license fee. They argued that many people buried there were poor and that pauper burials brought the cemetery little income. The request shows the pressure on a Black-controlled burial ground to provide low-cost funerals while meeting city expenses during a national economic crisis.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead

events.title: John Wesley Dobbs dies as Atlanta schools desegregate
events.description: John Wesley Dobbs died on August 30, 1961, as Atlanta’s public schools began admitting their first Black students. A railway mail clerk for thirty-two years and leader of Georgia’s Prince Hall Masons, he built civic organizations that pressed for Black political influence. In 1946 he and attorney A. T. Walden helped form the Atlanta Negro Voters League to coordinate voter registration and political action.
events.sourceLabel: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute: John Wesley Dobbs

events.title: Jean Childs Young dies after decades of education and children’s advocacy
events.description: Jean Childs Young died of cancer in Atlanta on September 16, 1994. Born in Marion, Alabama, on July 1, 1933, she studied elementary education at Manchester College and became a teacher. She worked in Georgia and Connecticut, trained teachers for low-income communities, and helped develop lessons for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference’s citizenship schools, which prepared adults for civic participation.
events.sourceLabel: New Georgia Encyclopedia: Jean Childs Young

events.title: The Brown family angel falls on the day Virginia Berry dies
events.description: Virginia Brown Akridge Berry was an Atlanta art teacher educated at Spelman, Columbia University, and Atlanta University. She placed a stone angel on the Brown family lot at South-View. On September 26, 1980, cemetery historian Albert H. Watts recalled, the angel fell from its pedestal around noon, breaking its head and wrist. Berry died at home that evening.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead

events.title: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson dies after building SNCC’s field operations
events.description: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson died of cancer on October 7, 1967, at twenty-five. A Spelman student, she joined Atlanta’s sit-ins, served thirty days in jail during the 1961 Rock Hill campaign, and was imprisoned for forty-five days at Mississippi’s Parchman Penitentiary after a Freedom Ride. These arrests did not push her out of the movement; she returned to the work of organizing it.
events.sourceLabel: SNCC Digital Gateway: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson

events.title: Amos Rucker dies and is buried at South-View
events.description: Amos Rucker died in Atlanta on October 10, 1905, and was buried at South-View two days later. Enslaved by the Rucker family, he accompanied a young white man into Confederate service as an army servant. After emancipation, Rucker worked in Atlanta and became a familiar member of the W. H. T. Walker Confederate veterans’ camp. Former governor Allen D. Candler and Confederate veterans joined his funeral; former Confederate general Clement A. Evans conducted the service, and Rucker was dressed in gray with a Confederate flag placed over his coffin.
events.source: City of the Dead, chapter 15, OCR page estimate 170; date shown in a burial-record caption.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 155–156; catalog record

events.title: Walter Drake Westmoreland is shot down over Hungary
events.description: First Lieutenant Walter Drake Westmoreland was killed on October 13, 1944, when German antiaircraft fire struck his P-51 near Lake Balaton, Hungary. He was returning from an escort mission to the Blechhammer oil refinery. Westmoreland, an Atlanta native, flew with the 302nd Fighter Squadron of the 332nd Fighter Group; the Air Force record identifies his Mustang as Dopey.
events.source: City of the Dead, chapter 15, OCR page estimate 266.
events.sourceLabel: National Museum of the U.S. Air Force — Walter Westmoreland with Dopey

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is awarded the Nobel Peace Prize
events.description: On October 14, 1964, Coretta Scott King telephoned her husband in an Atlanta hospital with news that he had been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. At thirty-five, Martin Luther King Jr. was the youngest man to receive the award at that time. He accepted it in Oslo on December 10, dedicating it to the people risking their safety to challenge segregation, and shared the prize money among civil-rights organizations.
events.sourceLabel: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford — Nobel Peace Prize

events.title: John W. E. Bowen calls for education and opportunity at Atlanta’s exposition
events.description: On October 21, 1895, theologian John Wesley Edward Bowen delivered “An Appeal to the King” during Negro Day at Atlanta’s Cotton States and International Exposition. He praised Black Americans’ achievements since emancipation and pressed for education and fuller opportunity. His address spoke to the limits imposed on Black life even as the exposition presented itself as a showcase of regional progress.
events.sourceLabel: Civil Rights Digital Library — An Appeal to the King, 1895 pamphlet

events.title: Sterling Watts is buried in Westview’s segregated Rest Haven section
events.description: Sterling Watts was buried in Rest Haven, the section of Atlanta’s Westview Cemetery set aside for African Americans, on October 26, 1885. His son Albert Watts was among the Black Atlantans who soon organized a cemetery under Black community ownership. South-View’s founders sought a place where Black families could make decisions about burial and care themselves.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1; catalog record

events.title: Wade Hampton is executed and buried at South-View
events.description: Wade Hampton was nineteen when he was hanged at Atlanta’s Fulton County jail, known as the Tower, on November 9, 1898. Imprisoned as a child for burglary, he had been leased to work at the Chattahoochee Brick Company, where an explosion cost him a leg. He was later convicted of killing another young prisoner and sentenced to death.
events.source: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 12, section “Am I Born to Die?,” OCR page estimate 135.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 12, pp. 120–121; catalog record

events.title: A young descendant unveils Bishop Lucius Holsey’s monument
events.description: On November 17, 1927, a five-year-old great-granddaughter unveiled a marble monument to Bishop Lucius Henry Holsey at South-View. About five hundred people attended, many arriving by special streetcars and buses. Black Methodist congregations had raised funds for the memorial, which honored Holsey as a bishop, preacher and orator.
events.source: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 11, Holsey section, OCR page estimate 147.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 11; catalog record

events.title: Montgomery’s Black residents begin a bus boycott and form the MIA
events.description: On December 5, 1955, about 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black residents stayed off the buses after Rosa Parks’s arrest four days earlier. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council had printed and distributed leaflets calling for the one-day protest. That afternoon, local ministers and organizers formed the Montgomery Improvement Association and elected the young Dexter Avenue Baptist Church pastor Martin Luther King Jr. as president.
events.sourceLabel: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford — Montgomery Bus Boycott

events.title: South-View co-founder Charles H. Morgan is buried
events.description: Charles H. Morgan was buried at South-View on December 17, 1886, eleven days after the cemetery’s stock book recorded his purchase of three shares. Morgan was a grocer, property owner and charter petitioner for the new cemetery. His family lot became one of the early burial places at the institution he had helped establish.
events.sourceLabel: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3; catalog record

events.title: Educator and scholar Horace Mann Bond dies
events.description: Horace Mann Bond died on December 21, 1972, after retiring the previous year from Atlanta University. Born in Nashville on November 8, 1904, into a family of educators and ministers, he entered Lincoln University at fourteen and later earned a doctorate at the University of Chicago. He led Fort Valley State College and became Lincoln University’s first Black president before returning to Atlanta as a dean and education researcher.
events.sourceLabel: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Horace Mann Bond

events.title: Librarian Annie L. McPheeters dies after building Atlanta’s Black history collection
events.description: Annie L. McPheeters died on December 23, 1994, at eighty-six, months after the Auburn Avenue Research Library opened in Atlanta. Born Annie Lou Watters in Floyd County on February 22, 1908, she joined the Auburn Branch as an assistant librarian in 1934. She developed its Negro History Collection, gathering books and resources about people of African descent that became a foundation for the later research library.
events.sourceLabel: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Annie L. McPheeters

events.title: Lillian Miles Lewis dies after a career in libraries and public service
events.description: Lillian Miles Lewis died in Atlanta on December 31, 2012, at seventy-three. A trained librarian, she worked at Atlanta University and later held leadership posts at Clark Atlanta University, including directing external affairs in its research office. She also served on Georgia’s State Ethics Commission and contributed to civic and professional organizations.
events.sourceLabel: American Library Association — Memorial resolution for Lillian Miles Lewis
